A scalar is defined by **how it behaves when the axes are rotated**, not by its sign, its
constancy or its conservation.
**Step 1 — state the definition.** A quantity is a **scalar** if it is specified by a
magnitude alone, with no direction - and the operational test is that every observer,
however they orient their coordinate axes, assigns it the **same value** ✓ That is
exactly the fourth option.
**Step 2 — contrast it with a vector.** A vector's **components** change when the axes
are rotated: a displacement of 5 m east is (5, 0) to one observer and (3, 4) to another
whose axes are turned through 37° ✓ A scalar such as mass or temperature has no
components to change, so its single value is the same for both.
**Why "conserved" is wrong.** Conservation and scalarity are unrelated ✗ **Momentum** is
conserved and is a **vector**; **kinetic energy** is a scalar and is **not** conserved in
an inelastic collision ✓ Each half of the claim fails.
**Why "never negative" is wrong.** Plenty of scalars are routinely negative ✗ -
temperature in °C, electric potential near a negative charge, gravitational potential
energy below the reference level, and electric charge itself ✓ A scalar may carry a sign;
what it cannot carry is a **direction**.
**Why "does not vary from point to point" is wrong.** That describes a **uniform** field,
not a scalar ✗ Temperature in a room, pressure in the atmosphere and potential around a
charge are all scalars that vary from place to place ✓ Such a varying scalar is called a
**scalar field**, and the term would be meaningless if scalars had to be constant.
**The common thread in the three wrong options.** Each takes some incidental property
that **some** scalars happen to have and promotes it to a definition ✓ Only
rotational invariance picks out scalars exactly.
**A test you can apply.** Ask: if I turn my axes by 90°, does the number change? If not,
it is a scalar ✓ Mass, time, charge, energy, temperature and speed all pass; velocity,
force, displacement and torque all fail.
∴ a scalar quantity has the same value for observers with different orientations of the
axes.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, that a scalar can never be negative.
Temperature in °C, electric potential and electric charge are all scalars that take
negative values, so that statement is false. The key has been corrected to the fourth
option.

Sort the list by asking of each quantity: **does it need a direction?**
**Step 1 — work down the list.**
**pressure** - force per unit area, but it acts equally in all directions at a point in a
fluid and is specified by one number: **scalar** ✓
**power** - rate of doing work, a single number in watts: **scalar**
**energy** - a single number in joules: **scalar**
**impulse** - F̄Δt, equal to the **change in momentum**, which has a direction:
**vector** ✓
**gravitational potential** - potential energy per unit mass, a single number: **scalar**
(note that gravitational **field** is a vector, but potential is not)
**electrical charge** - a number with a sign, but no direction: **scalar**
**temperature** - a single number: **scalar**
**area** - can be given a direction, the **outward normal** to the surface: **vector** ✓
**Step 2 — collect the vectors.** Only **impulse and area** ✓
**Why area is a vector.** A plane area is represented by a vector of magnitude equal to
the area, pointing along the **normal** to the surface ✓ This is what makes flux, Φ =
B̄·Ā, meaningful, and it is why the orientation of a coil matters in electromagnetic
induction. Without the direction, "area" could not distinguish a coil facing the field
from one edge-on to it.
**Why pressure is not a vector despite coming from force.** The force on a surface is
F̄ = P Ā: the **direction** belongs to the area vector, and P is the scalar that scales
it ✓ Pressure at a point in a fluid has no preferred direction at all - it pushes equally
every way, which is Pascal's principle.
**Why charge is not a vector despite having a sign.** A sign is not a direction ✓ A
negative charge is not "charge pointing backwards"; adding charges is ordinary
arithmetic, with no components and no parallelogram law.
**Reading the distractors.** Every other option includes **pressure** or **gravitational
potential** among the vectors ✗ and both are scalars for the reasons given ✓
**The test to carry away.** A quantity is a vector only if it obeys the **triangle law of
addition** and has a direction ✓ Impulse and area both do; the rest of the list does not.
∴ impulse and area.

pradeep|Physics|0|7|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Constant **speed** constrains path length only - it says nothing about direction, so
every claim involving direction must fail.
**Step 1 — write down what is given.** |v̄| = v₀ at every instant, a positive constant.
The **direction** of v̄ is entirely unconstrained.
**Step 2 — test each statement against a counterexample.** Take uniform circular motion,
which has constant speed and is the natural test case.
**(a) "The average velocity is not zero at any time"** ✗ Over one complete revolution the
particle returns to its start, so the displacement is zero and the **average velocity is
zero** ✓ The claim fails.
**(b) "Average acceleration must always vanish"** ✗ Over a **half** revolution the
velocity reverses, from v₀ to −v₀, so the average acceleration is 2v₀/(T/2) ≠ 0 ✓ The
claim fails.
**(c) "Displacements in equal time intervals are equal"** ✗ Displacement is a vector.
In circular motion the particle moves north in one quarter-period and west in the next:
equal in **magnitude**, but different vectors ✓ The claim fails.
**(d) "Equal path lengths are traversed in equal intervals"** ✓ Path length is
distance = speed x time = v₀ Δt, and since v₀ is the same at every instant, equal
intervals give equal distances **always**, whatever the path ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the last statement is **necessarily** true.
**Why this is the only safe statement.** Speed is the **magnitude** of velocity, and
distance is the integral of speed ✓ So a constraint on speed translates directly into a
constraint on distance - and into nothing else. Everything involving displacement,
velocity or acceleration involves direction, which is free to change however it likes.
**A second counterexample, to be sure.** A particle moving along a zigzag at constant
speed: after each equal time interval it has covered the same **path length**, yet its
displacement swings about and its average velocity varies from interval to interval ✓
**The distinction at the heart of it.**
**distance / speed** - scalars, fixed here
**displacement / velocity / acceleration** - vectors, unconstrained here
∴ equal path lengths are traversed in equal intervals.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, that displacements in equal intervals are
equal. Displacement is a vector, and in circular motion at constant speed successive
quarter-period displacements point in different directions, so they are not equal. The
key has been corrected to the fourth option.

pradeep|Physics|0|8|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration - it means the acceleration is
**perpendicular to the velocity**, and in two-dimensional motion both lie in the plane.
**Step 1 — see why the acceleration need not be zero.** Differentiate v̄·v̄ = v₀²:
2 v̄·ā = 0
so
**v̄ ⟂ ā** ✓
The acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity, but it may perfectly well be non-zero -
uniform circular motion is the standard example, with |ā| = v₀²/r ✓
**Step 2 — see where that acceleration must point.** The motion is **two dimensional**,
so the position and the velocity lie in a fixed plane at all times. Differentiating a
vector that stays in a plane gives a vector in the **same plane**, so
**ā lies in the plane of the motion** ✓ necessarily and always.
**Step 3 — test the remaining claims.**
**"The acceleration is zero"** ✗ refuted by uniform circular motion, where the speed is
constant and the acceleration is v₀²/r.
**"The acceleration is bounded"** ✗ The acceleration is v₀²/ρ, where ρ is the radius of
curvature of the path. A path may curve as sharply as it likes - ρ can approach zero -
and then the acceleration grows without limit ✓ Nothing in the problem bounds the
curvature, so this is not **necessarily** true.
**"The particle must be undergoing uniform circular motion"** ✗ A circle is only one of
infinitely many constant-speed paths. A particle may traverse an ellipse, a spiral or any
smooth curve at constant speed ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Only "the acceleration is necessarily in the plane of motion" is
forced by the given information ✓
**Why "necessarily" is the operative word.** Several options describe things that **can**
happen; the question asks what **must** ✓ One counterexample is enough to destroy a claim,
and uniform circular motion or a tightening spiral supplies one for each of the others.
**The geometry worth remembering.** For any motion, the acceleration splits into
**tangential** a_t = dv/dt, which changes the speed - here **zero**
**normal** a_n = v²/ρ, which changes the direction - here all of it ✓
With the speed constant, the whole acceleration is the normal part, pointing towards the
centre of curvature, which lies in the plane of the curve.
∴ the acceleration of the particle is necessarily in the plane of motion.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, that the acceleration is zero. A particle
in uniform circular motion has constant speed and acceleration v₀²/r ≠ 0, so that is
false. The key has been corrected to the third option.
